---
title: "Findable, Not Simple"
abstract: |
  Accounts of why induction works say what the world must be like for it to work, and the usual answer is that the world must be simple: its regularities must have short descriptions. I argue that this is the wrong property. What an inquirer needs is regularities that can be found at a cost she can pay, and the two properties come apart. Under a standard cryptographic assumption there are pairs of hypotheses of equal description length such that an inquirer with unlimited computation separates them given a few bits more than the seed holds, while no feasible method separates them from chance with any amount of data. Three consequences follow. Underdetermination has a third kind, indexed to resources, which more evidence does not cure. Induction rests on a contingent premise about computational accessibility, one that the success of science supports only in the domains where we looked. And the Bayesian ideal is not a norm for feasible inquirers in such cases: no feasible credence is more accurate than a coin flip, though the ideal credence is nearly perfect. I separate what depends on the cryptographic assumption from what does not, and ask whether nature contains the structure.

# Two properties of a law {#sec-intro}

Evidence supports a law only if the world is some way, and Hume showed that the evidence cannot certify the way. The formal defences of induction accept this and prove conditionals. If the source of the data is computable, the total expected error of Solomonoff's predictor is bounded by a multiple of the source's description length [@RathmannerHutter2011]. If the target concept has a short description, any short hypothesis consistent with a sample of moderate size is probably approximately correct [@Valiant1984; @Blumer1987]. If the truth is the simplest theory compatible with the evidence so far, conjecturing the simplest such theory is the way to converge to the truth with the fewest retractions [@Kelly2007]. The conditions differ, but each says that the world must be simple, and a common gloss on the success of science is that the world is.

I argue that the gloss misidentifies the property. Distinguish the *description length* of a law, the length of the shortest program that generates the data, from its *findability*, the cost of the cheapest method that recovers from the data a law predicting the rest. A short law can be found only by searching through shorter ones, at a cost exponential in its length. The two properties come apart, and when they do the justifications above are silent about the cases in which an inquirer like us would need them. The thesis is this: *what induction needs from the world is that the regularities that matter be findable by feasible methods; that is a contingent premise distinct from simplicity, and it does the work that simplicity is credited with.*

Section 2 shows where the standard justifications use findability under another name, Section 3 states the contrast and measures it, Section 4 draws the consequence for credence, Section 5 for underdetermination, Section 6 for the premise induction needs, and Section 7 answers objections.

None of the ingredients is new. That pseudorandom functions cannot be learned by efficient learners is due to Kearns and Valiant, building on [@GGM1986] (their argument is the one I use [@KearnsValiant1994]). Aaronson draws the epistemological moral: given pseudorandom generators, "learning is impossible purely because of computational complexity" and not for want of data [@Aaronson2013, sec. 7.1]. Barrett and Huttegger argue that, depending on one's computational resources, no evidence may decide whether a notion of randomness describes one's data, so that fundamentally stochastic theories face a radical underdetermination [@BarrettHuttegger2020]. Eagle defines randomness as unpredictability relative to a predictor and rejects a split between pseudo-random and genuinely random processes [@Eagle2005]. Peirce held that the simpler hypothesis is "the more facile and natural" one, because without a natural bent matching nature's there is no chance of understanding it [@Peirce1908]. Sterkenburg argues that effectiveness rather than simplicity does the work in Solomonoff's account, and is more naturally a constraint on us than on the world [@Sterkenburg2016]; Herrmann that the PAC Occam theorem hides a similarity condition [@Herrmann2020]. Impagliazzo and Levin, and later Liu and Pass, prove equivalences between one-way functions and the infeasibility of extrapolation and of approximating time-bounded Kolmogorov complexity [@ImpagliazzoLevin1990; @LiuPass2020]. Garrabrant and colleagues define credences relative to the resources of those who might exploit them [@Garrabrant2016].

What the paper adds to these is fivefold. It shows that the three justifications above each contain a findability premise under another name, and that the premise is not effectiveness, which is too weak, but feasibility. It proves that feasible credences are no more accurate than chance in the hard cases while the ideal is nearly perfect, which defeats the standard reply that the ideal is a gold standard to be approximated (@sec-credence). It identifies the premise exactly, for the Solomonoff-style class of feasible laws, with a statement whose negation is the existence of one-way functions (@sec-premise). It answers the objection from abduction with a count of the bits a candidate theory must come from (@sec-objections). And it offers a criterion for findability, partial credit, which the measurements in @sec-same illustrate. I do not find the thesis stated in any one of the sources above.

# What the razor's guarantees cover {#sec-razor}

Each of the three results compares a method with a target that is short, and each hides a clause about the method.

Solomonoff's predictor is a mixture over all computable sources, weighted by $2^{-K}$ where $K$ is description length. Its error bound is $K(\mu)\ln 2$ plus a constant for any source $\mu$ in the class [@RathmannerHutter2011]. The predictor is not computable. Rathmanner and Hutter say so, and defend its use as a "gold standard", an optimum known but not attainable, in the way that full minimax search is for chess: since in practice only feasible approximations are considered, what matters is to find approximations that are useful [@RathmannerHutter2011, sec. 9.1]. That defence has a condition: the ideal must be approachable by feasible approximations. I show in @sec-credence that in the cases at issue it is not. Sterkenburg argues that the guarantee comes from the effectiveness of the mixture and not from any preference for simplicity, and that effectiveness is more naturally read as a constraint on our own capacities than on the world [@Sterkenburg2016]. I agree and add an interaction. Effectiveness is computability, and it costs nothing to satisfy in the limit. The constraint that bites is feasibility, and whether a constraint on our capacities is met well enough depends on how the world's regularities are structured.

The PAC Occam theorem has the same structure. It says that a hypothesis consistent with the sample and describable in few bits generalises. It is applied through an *Occam algorithm*, a procedure that outputs such a hypothesis, and the learning-theoretic version requires that the procedure run in polynomial time [@Valiant1984; @Blumer1987; see @Herrmann2020]. The existence of an Occam algorithm for a concept class is therefore a findability premise. The description-length clause tells us that if we find a short consistent hypothesis, it is good. It does not tell us that we can find one. Aaronson notes the same gap in the basic PAC theorem, which "gives us no clues about how to find a hypothesis" consistent with the data [@Aaronson2013, sec. 7.1]. Herrmann, for his part, shows that the theorem has a matching anti-Occam theorem and that its applicability depends on a condition on how training and test cases are related [@Herrmann2020]. I add that the Occam algorithm is the place where the cost of search enters the theory, and that nothing in the notion of simplicity bounds that cost.

Kelly's razor is the one defence that does not mention computation. His measure of cost is errors, retractions and the times at which they occur, and he argues that the razor is the optimal policy for those costs [@Kelly2007; @KellySchulteJuhl1997]. This is a claim about the logic of convergence, and it is silent on the effort to produce the next conjecture. The guarantee holds if the method can name the simplest theory compatible with the data. If naming it requires a search of exponential size, a method that is optimal in retractions is not one anyone can run. I do not suggest that Kelly's analysis is wrong. It is an analysis of one cost, and the argument below concerns another.

The three have this in common: each states a relation between a method and a target, and then takes the *method* for granted. The assumption is that someone can produce the shortest consistent program, the Occam hypothesis or the simplest compatible theory. For a bounded inquirer the assumption is a premise about the world: whether the short thing can be reached from the data.

# Same description, different cost {#sec-same}

Take a generator $G$ that maps a $k$-bit seed to an $m$-bit string, computable in time polynomial in $m$. Two hypotheses about an observed string $x$ of length $m$: $H_G$, that $x=G(s)$ for a seed $s$ drawn uniformly, and $H_U$, that $x$ is drawn uniformly. Under $H_G$ the data have a description of about $k$ bits plus the fixed length of $G$. Under $H_U$ they have, with overwhelming probability, none shorter than about $m$. This is the cleanest version of the contrast between a deterministic law with a short seed and a chance process. A rival to a short law is, in the first place, chance.

**Proposition 1** (unbounded inquirers). *Let $m=k+c$. The test "$x$ lies in the range of $G$" accepts with probability 1 under $H_G$ and with probability at most $2^{-c}$ under $H_U$. With equal priors, acceptance raises the odds on $H_G$ to at least $2^{c}:1$. The test costs $2^k$ evaluations of $G$.*

The proof is a count: the range has at most $2^k$ points among $2^m$. Fifteen more bits of data than the seed has give odds above thirty thousand to one, and the enumeration yields the seed.

**Proposition 2** (feasible inquirers). *Say $G$ is a pseudorandom generator if for every polynomial-time probabilistic procedure $D$, the difference between $\Pr[D(G(s))=1]$ and $\Pr[D(u)=1]$ is smaller than the reciprocal of every polynomial in $k$, for large $k$. Pseudorandom generators exist if and only if one-way functions do [@HILL1999], and the notion goes back to Blum and Micali [-@BlumMicali1984]. Assume one exists, for polynomial stretch. Then no polynomial-time procedure distinguishes $H_G$ from $H_U$ with non-negligible advantage, however long the string.*

That is the definition of the assumption, not a result of mine; I state it because the rest depends on its quantifiers. The inquirer's data are unlimited; her time is polynomial. The point is of a different kind from the standard problem of induction, because the failure is not one of insufficient evidence. The evidence settles the question: Proposition 1 shows that $k+15$ bits do. What is missing is a feasible route from evidence to answer. Experiment does not supply one. Pseudorandom function families, which are indistinguishable from random functions by feasible procedures that choose their own queries [@GGM1986], put the same barrier in front of an inquirer who intervenes, and Aaronson makes the corresponding point about learning them [@Aaronson2013, sec. 7.1].

**What is conditional, and on what.** Proposition 1 is unconditional. Proposition 2 is conditional on the existence of one-way functions, which implies $P\neq NP$ and is believed by cryptographers but unproved. Two weaker facts need less. If the seed length is logarithmic in $m$, brute force is polynomial and the separation fails; the gap needs $k$ to grow. And for any fixed key size the question is about the concrete cost of the best attack; the asymptotic theorem says nothing about whether a given 128-bit instance is hard, and I make no such claim about real instances. What the asymptotic result establishes is the *possibility* of the separation, which is all that a refutation of the claim "short implies findable" requires.

**Measurements.** The demonstration (script and logs accompany the paper) generates strings from three sources, each specified by a short seed, and compares unbounded and bounded methods. It illustrates; it does not prove. For $H_G$ I use SHA-256 in counter mode keyed by a $d$-bit seed, a stand-in for a pseudorandom generator rather than a proven one. The brute-force test recovers the seed in every trial, and the cost doubles with each added seed bit.

| Seed bits $d$ | 12 | 16 | 20 | 22 | 24 |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Full scan, seconds | 0.002 | 0.04 | 0.66 | 2.6 | 10.6 |

Extrapolated, a 48-bit seed would take about five years on the same machine, and a 128-bit seed more than the age of the universe. The data needed are as predicted. At $d=12$ the fraction of chance strings that accidentally match some seed falls from 0.23 at 14 bits of data to 0.001 at 22, against the predicted $2^{12-n}$ (0.25 and 0.001).

Standard learners do no better than the toss of a coin on the hash stream, each trained to predict the next bit from the preceding 48, on a stream of 200,000 bits, 80 percent for training. Logistic regression, gradient boosting and a small neural network all score 0.50 predicting the next bit, as they do on uniform random bits. This is not evidence that nothing feasible works, only the expected behaviour of the usual tools.

The same description length does not always mean the same findability, and the demonstration includes two cases where it does not. A linear feedback shift register (LFSR) with an $L$-bit state is also specified by a short seed: its feedback taps and initial state, about $2L$ bits. The Berlekamp–Massey algorithm [@Massey1969] recovers the register from $2L$ output bits in time quadratic in $L$ and then predicts every later bit exactly. The measurement: $L=20$ in 0.002 seconds, $L=256$ in 0.03, $L=1024$ in 0.3, with the next 2,000 bits predicted exactly in each case. A 48-bit LFSR seed is found in milliseconds and a 2,048-bit one in a third of a second; a 48-bit hash seed would take years. The longer description is the more findable. The Geffe generator combines three registers by a nonlinear rule. Its description is $3L$ state bits, and brute force costs $2^{3L}$; but the output agrees with each of two registers three quarters of the time, so each can be attacked separately for a cost of about $3\cdot 2^{L}$. At $L=16$ the divide-and-conquer attack recovers all three registers with about $2\times10^5$ evaluations where brute force needs $3\times10^{14}$.

A caution from the measurements. Generic learners also do something I had not expected. On a 24-bit LFSR with a 48-bit seed, a small neural network predicted the next bit with accuracy 1.00 from a 48-bit window of earlier bits, whether the register had 3, 5, 7, 11 or 15 taps. Gradient boosting managed this for 3 taps and scored between 0.51 and 0.69 for the others; logistic regression stayed at chance. So findability depends on the class of methods as well as on the source: the LFSR stream is findable by a method class that includes simple neural networks and by a specialised algorithm, and not by every method. The pseudorandom generator is the case where it is not findable by *any* feasible method; the demonstration does not show that, and cannot.

**A criterion.** What distinguishes the three cases is the structure of the search space. For the LFSR, a wrong guess about the taps yields output correlated with the right one in a way that linear algebra exploits. For Geffe, each component correlates with the output and can be found by itself. For the hash, a seed that is one bit wrong gives output uncorrelated with the truth: a partial guess earns nothing. A law is findable to the extent that its approximations reward partial guesses, so that the inquirer can climb, decompose or solve. This suggests that findability is a property of the relation between a law and a class of methods, which is graded. I offer it as a characterisation and not as a theorem: for specific classes, such as parities under statistical-query methods, the lower bounds are known, but a general criterion is beyond what the measurements show [@ShalevShwartz2017].

The contrast, then, is between two things that the justifications of induction run together. Short description tells us how few bits of data suffice for an unbounded inquirer, and it governs sample complexity. Findability tells us how much work the inquirer must do, and it governs computational complexity. Learning theory has long distinguished the two, and the result I use is that they are independent under cryptographic assumptions: a statistically easy problem can be computationally hopeless [@KearnsValiant1994].

# What a feasible inquirer should believe {#sec-credence}

The Bayesian reply to the last section is that the right credence in the face of evidence $x$ is the posterior on the true likelihoods, whether or not anyone can compute it. In the two-hypothesis case the posterior is at least $1/(1+2^{-c})$ on strings in the range of $G$ and zero off it. Ideals are often uncomputable; what matters is that a credence is better the nearer it is to the ideal.

I accept the evaluative claim and ask what it licenses. The ideal is usually offered as a target for approximation, which is how Rathmanner and Hutter use it. That use presupposes that feasible approximations come close to the ideal in the respect that matters, and for credences the respect is accuracy. Here that presupposition fails, and fails completely.

**Proposition 3.** *Let $c(x)\in[0,1]$ be a credence in $H_G$ computed by a polynomial-time probabilistic procedure. Score it by expected Brier inaccuracy with equal priors, $B(c)=\tfrac12E_G[(c-1)^2]+\tfrac12E_U[c^2]$. Write $\Delta=E_G[c]-E_U[c]$ and $\delta=E_G[c^2]-E_U[c^2]$. Then*
$$B(c)=\tfrac12-E_U[c(1-c)]-\Delta+\tfrac12\delta\ \ge\ \tfrac14-|\Delta|-\tfrac12|\delta|.$$
*If $G$ is pseudorandom, $\Delta$ and $\delta$ are negligible, so no feasible credence has inaccuracy below $\tfrac14$ by more than a negligible amount, which the constant credence $\tfrac12$ attains. The ideal posterior has inaccuracy at most $2^{-c}$.*

The identity follows by expanding the squares, and the inequality from $c(1-c)\le\tfrac14$. The quantity $\Delta$ is the advantage of a feasible test that outputs 1 with probability $c(x)$, and $\delta$ that of a test that outputs 1 with probability $c(x)^2$, so Proposition 2 makes both negligible. For the ideal $c^*$: it vanishes off the range, whose $H_U$-probability is at most $2^{-c}$, and on the range $1-c^*\le 2^{-c}$. (I checked the identity numerically on random distributions.)

Two consequences. First, no feasible procedure approximates the posterior, since one that did would beat the constant. The "gold standard" defence needs approximations that are useful, and here there are none, so the ideal is not a target for anyone who must compute. Second, accuracy-based arguments for probabilism [@Joyce1998] rank credences by closeness to the truth. By that ranking an inquirer who gives $H_G$ and $H_U$ equal credence is as accurate as any feasible inquirer can be, whichever is true. She is not irrational; she is wrong only by the lights of a standard that nothing she could do would meet.

The Bayesian faces a dilemma. If the ideal is merely an evaluative standard, Solomonoff's theorem explains why an ideal agent succeeds, and the practice of agents who cannot compute the ideal is left unexplained. If it is a guide, because it can be approximated, then approximability is a premise about the world, namely that the posterior is feasibly approximable on the hypotheses that matter, and the premise is false of the pair above. The defender of the first horn may reply that norms need not guide. I agree, and conclude that the credence norm that explains and justifies *our* success must be formulated for feasible agents. The natural formulation indexes support to a class of methods: the evidence supports $H$ over $H'$ for $\mathcal C$ to the degree that the best method in $\mathcal C$ can use it to tell them apart. Garrabrant and colleagues give the formal model for a case that is, in this respect, parallel: credences are required to be unexploitable by traders of bounded efficiency, and a sequence from which no efficiently computable procedure can single out a subsequence of different frequency counts as pseudorandom, and the market learns its frequency [@Garrabrant2016]. Their setting is logical uncertainty; the move from the ideal to the unexploited is the one I recommend for empirical uncertainty.

# Underdetermination indexed to resources {#sec-under}

Standard taxonomies divide underdetermination into holist and contrastive, and into transient and permanent: the evidence we now have fails to decide between theories, or no possible evidence would [@Stanford2023]. Against the permanent kind, realists point out that indirect evidence can break the tie. Werndl uses the idea, due to Laudan and Leplin, to choose between deterministic and indeterministic models that are observationally equivalent at finite precision [@Werndl2015].

The pair above is neither transient nor permanent. It is not permanent because $k+15$ bits decide it. It is not transient in the usual sense because no new kind of evidence is wanted and more of the same does nothing for a feasible inquirer, whatever the amount. It is a third kind: *underdetermined for a class of inquirers and determined for a wider one*. The distinction matters because the realist reply to underdetermination relies on the limit of inquiry, in which idealised inquirers have all the evidence there will be. For feasible inquirers that limit does not separate the pair.

Three clarifications. The index is a model and not a measure of human power: polynomial time, quantum polynomial time and a polynomial-time inquirer holding side information define different classes, and the relation of underdetermination changes with the class. Barrett and Huttegger reach a nearby conclusion from algorithmic randomness: which notion of randomness describes the data may be impossible to determine with the available computational resources [@BarrettHuttegger2020]. Their result concerns infinite sequences and the comparison of randomness notions, and the present one concerns finite data and the comparison of a law with chance, but the lesson is related, and Eagle's relativisation of randomness to a predictor is its conceptual root [@Eagle2005]. Second, the case is not confined to toy generators. Harlow and Hayden argue that the quantum computations required by the thought experiments used against smooth black-hole horizons take time exponential in the black hole's entropy, which prevents the experiments from being done for a wide variety of black holes [@HarlowHayden2013]. Whatever the verdict on firewalls, it is a case in which an argument in physics puts a distinction behind an exponential computation. Third, the thesis is about evidence and not about truth. A realist can hold that $H_G$ is true or $H_U$ is, and that the fact does not wait on us. What the third kind of underdetermination removes is her ability to say that the evidence, accumulated, would show which. A theory of confirmation that treats support as a relation between hypotheses and data alone cannot register this, and must take a second argument.

# The premise induction needs {#sec-premise}

Call *findability* the premise that, in the domain under inquiry, feasible methods applied to feasible amounts of data recover laws that predict well. It is distinct from simplicity, since each can hold without the other. Hash outputs have a short description and are unfindable; a register with a 2,048-bit seed has a long description and, as @sec-same showed, is found in a third of a second. It is also contingent. The question is what we know about it.

**A mathematical part.** Consider the Solomonoff-style class: all laws that run in polynomial time, weighted by description length. Impagliazzo and Levin consider *universal extrapolation*: given a prefix produced by a polynomial-time machine on a random tape, sample a continuation from the machine's own distribution. This is posterior prediction for a law whose randomness is unknown, and it is possible for every such machine if and only if one-way functions do not exist [@ImpagliazzoLevin1990; as reported in @LiuPass2020]. So a findability claim that covers every feasible law, on average over the law's randomness, is equivalent to the negation of the central assumption of cryptography. Liu and Pass show the same from another side: one-way functions exist if and only if computing time-bounded Kolmogorov complexity, the length of the shortest feasible description of data, is mildly hard on average, even to approximate [@LiuPass2020]. Finding the best short description of random-looking data is exactly the task that cryptography presumes to be hard. I take this to be the sharpest statement of how findability and simplicity separate: the Solomonoff programme, restricted to feasible laws, is the study of an inversion problem whose hardness is the foundation of cryptography.

A dichotomy follows, and its structure does not depend on which way the mathematics falls. If one-way functions do not exist, findability holds for every feasible law, and induction for feasible inquirers is vindicated by a theorem of complexity theory, in which simplicity plays no part. If they exist, then findability fails for some feasible laws, and any justification of induction needs a premise about *which* laws the world instantiates. Nanashima proves a dichotomy of the second sort at the level of learning: for any class of efficiently computable concepts, either it is heuristically learnable or auxiliary-input one-way functions exist [@Nanashima2021]. Failures of heuristic learnability are, in this sense, always cryptographic in form.

**An empirical part.** Given the second branch, what is the evidence for findability in our world? The tempting answer is the success of science. But success is evidence about findability only in the domains where we looked, and the unfindable leaves no record of itself. A process we cannot compress is a process we call noise. Eagle holds that what counts as random is settled by the empirically successful theory appropriate to the phenomenon [@Eagle2005]. I take the moral to be that the classification of a process as random records, in part, what our theories have not captured. The residue of unfindable structure, if there is any, is therefore classified as chance, and the base rate at which we find structure in what we examine is the only evidence, and it is evidence restricted by selection. Nanashima notes that hard-to-learn "random" concepts seem empirically rare [@Nanashima2021]. I read that as a datum of the same kind: where learners are applied, they work, because that is where they are applied.

Three natural cases bear on the question, and I assess them as I see them. *Low-dimensional chaos* has a short deterministic law, and the data look like a random sequence, but the one-step law is smooth, so a guess near the truth predicts near the truth over short horizons, and the law can be recovered by methods that exploit that gradation. It is findable, and the observational equivalence of such systems with stochastic ones [@Werndl2015] is a matter of finite precision and not of cost. *Many-body systems* have descriptions so long that the data are shorter than the law, so $m<k$ and even an unbounded inquirer is stuck; the underdetermination is informational and not of the kind studied here. *Black-hole radiation* is the one case I know in which a physical argument places the distinction behind an exponential computation [@HarlowHayden2013]. The remaining instances are artefacts: seeded random number generators in simulations, hashed identifiers, ciphertext. In those the premise fails by design, and an inquirer who lacks the key faces precisely the pair above. I conclude that nothing known shows nature to contain unfindable structure, and nothing known shows it does not.

The two hypotheses, however, predict different patterns of success. Simplicity predicts that the laws we have found are short. Findability predicts that they come with graded approximations, such as perturbation series, effective theories and linearisations, which reward partial guesses, and that our failures cluster where such gradation is absent: turbulence, many-body systems, adversarial systems. My impression is that the record fits the second prediction better than the first, since shortness is a poor description of much of what has been found. The record is selected, and I offer the impression as the form a test would take.

Two remarks on the neighbouring literature. Peirce's thought that the simpler hypothesis is "the more facile and natural" one, because a mind not attuned to nature has no chance of understanding it, is the nearest ancestor of my thesis [@Peirce1908]. I add that attunement is not a feature of the mind alone: the same mind is attuned or not depending on how nature's regularities are structured, which is why it is a premise about the world. Lin, Tegmark and Rolnick explain why small neural networks approximate the functions of physics well, by symmetry, locality and low polynomial order, and set aside how rapidly the networks can be trained [@Lin2017]. That is the gap of this paper in a different vocabulary, since statistical efficiency and computational efficiency are separate, and the hardness of improper learning is established essentially only under cryptographic or average-case assumptions [@Daniely2014].

Schmidhuber's speed prior is a resource-based prior over laws that favours those that run fast, and he predicts that apparent randomness reflects short and fast pseudorandom generators [@Schmidhuber2000]. Fastness to run is not fastness to find. A short fast pseudorandom generator is the standard example of a law that is neither. The prediction is a hypothesis that apparent noise is law, which may be true, and which the arguments above show would be undetectable. Aaronson's proposal that the intractability of NP-complete problems be treated as a physical principle concerns what nature can compute [@Aaronson2005]. My question is what nature can hide.

# Objections {#sec-objections}

*Nature is not an adversary, and the pairs are gerrymandered.* The thesis is not that nature is hard but that findability is a premise. As to the pairs, the justifications under discussion quantify over all short programs or all short hypotheses, and the pairs belong to those classes; to restrict to natural laws is to concede that a premise about the world has been added. The restriction cannot be made by simplicity, since the excluded laws are as short as the included ones. Nanashima's dichotomy adds that unlearnability, wherever it occurs, implies auxiliary-input one-way functions [@Nanashima2021]. If nature contains hard structure, it is not a miscellany of awkward cases, since it is of one kind.

*The result is asymptotic and rests on unproved assumptions.* Granted, and in two places. Proposition 2 rests on one-way functions, a stronger assumption than $P\ne NP$ and one widely believed. And the theorem is silent on any particular instance: for a given 128-bit key the question is the cost of the best known attack, and I claim nothing about it. What the asymptotic result does establish is that "short implies findable" is not a logical or complexity-theoretic truth, because it is false under a standard assumption. The dichotomy of @sec-premise adds that the denial of the assumption makes findability a theorem, in a form that still leaves simplicity idle.

*Credence should track the true likelihood whatever is feasible.* This is the Bayesian horn already discussed in @sec-credence. The norm survives as an evaluation, and no feasible agent can follow it or approximate it in these cases, which means that it explains the ideal agent's success and not ours.

*Realism concerns truth and not discriminability.* Agreed, and @sec-under makes the point: the claim concerns what the evidence can do. It does bear on one argument. The inference from permanent underdetermination to anti-realism fails if the underdetermination is permanent only for inquirers of a given class. The converse inference, that realism is safe, fails as well, for the class that matters is ours.

*Cannot discriminate is not cannot know which is true: abduction.* A scientist who cannot test $H_G$ against $H_U$ by data can still choose the better explanation by simplicity, scope and fit. This is the strongest objection, and it fails for a reason that can be counted. To believe $H_G$ in the sense that matters, one must hold a particular law, which means a seed $s^*$, and a seed is $k$ bits. Theoretical virtues rank candidates, and verification is cheap: one computes $G$ forward on a proposed seed and compares. What they cannot do is supply the candidate. Before the data, the $2^k$ seeds are equally simple, equally broad and equally apt; after the data, one of them fits perfectly, and it stands out only when it is tried. The $k$ bits must therefore come from somewhere. They can come from the data, but extracting them is the cost the pseudorandom generator makes infeasible. They can come from the prior, in which case the inquirer already had the law, or from indirect evidence of the kind Werndl uses, which works by importing a candidate or a constraint from elsewhere. That is legitimate, and it confirms that findability is relative to side information. Or they can come from luck, at probability $2^{-(k-b)}$ for $b$ bits of luck. Abduction on a supplied candidate works; abduction as a source of candidates is search under another name. Where the structure rewards partial guesses, as with a register or a combiner, abduction and search coincide and succeed; where it does not, abduction has nothing to work on.

*Does the thesis prove too much?* If findability is needed for induction, and there is no guarantee of it, one might say induction is unjustified. That does not follow from the thesis, which says only what the justification must contain. Philosophers who accept that inductive justification rests on some premise about the world, simplicity or uniformity or the existence of natural kinds, lose nothing by being told that the premise they need is computational. The change is that the premise can now be studied: it has a mathematical component whose status is known, and an empirical component whose evidence is subject to a known selection effect. Simplicity, by contrast, governs only how much data suffice.
